newsitem.title: USA: Six more countries sign derivatives oversight pact.
newsitem.headline: Six more countries sign derivatives oversight pact.

text.p: Six more countries have signed an international pact designed to help avoid financial crises like the collapse of Barings in 1995, the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission said Wednesday.

Futures regulatory authorities in Brazil, Denmark, Hungary, Malaysia, Portugal and Sweden signed the Declaration on Cooperation and Supervision of International Futures Exchanges and Clearing Organizations, the CFTC said in a statement released at a derivatives conference here.

"The declaration and the complementary Memorandum of Understanding and Agreement...constitutes multilateral mechanisms for the sharing of information on a bilateral basis between the requesting and requested market authority consistent with their legal and contractual obligations," the release said.
Under the pact, the occurrence of certain agreed triggering events affecting an exchange member's financial resources or positions will prompt the sharing of information.
"The trigger levels are designed to facilitate the identification of large exposures by firms that could have a potentially adverse effect on markets," the CFTC said.
"The need for such information sharing was one of the lessons learned during the 1995 Barings crisis and reinforced in 1996 during events on the copper markets involving Sumitomo Corp," it said.
British investment bank Barings Plc collapsed in February 1995 under the weight of $790 million in unauthorized derivatives trades.
In June 1996, the world's biggest copper merchant, Sumitomo Corp, said it lost an estimated $1.8 billion over 10 years from unauthorized copper trades.
The CFTC issued the statement at the Futures Industry Association's annual conference in Boca Raton.
The original declaration was signed a year ago and now includes 62 international futures exchanges and clearing organizations.
Hungarian Banking and Capital Markets Supervisor
Comissao do Mercado de Valores Mobiliarios (Portugal)
